title: Part 3.I — The Dialectic of Constitutions
summary: Burke's longest chapter (79 pp.) is the master applied-dramatism worked example: a pentad-and-substance-vocabulary analysis of constitutional language addressed by Agents to Agents. The first third (pp.323-340) is methodological: it argues that human-relations theorizing requires a representative anecdote that is synecdochic rather than metonymic, rejects mind-body parallelism in favor of two-concentric-circles dialectic, treats total war as a candidate representative anecdote (war is the modern counterpart of the tribal festival and the agape), distinguishes constitutive from admonitory anecdotes and religious from secular futurism, and then settles on the Constitution itself as the master anecdote because constitutions are 'substantival' (constituere/statuere = to place, set, stand) and explicitly enact human wills. The remaining two thirds works seven applied cases — Herbert Read's anarcho-syndicalism, H. B. Parkes's modified laissez-faire, the spectrum from 'freedom' to 'capitalism' with money as 'God-term', Coleridge's Pantisocracy + 'The Ancient Mariner', Marshall's Marbury v. Madison argument for judicial review, the role of the President (Roosevelt as paradigm), and the Swiss federalist tradition as theorized by Denis de Rougemont. Five master moves recur: (a) every constitution presupposes a constitution-behind-the-constitution (an implicit Ultimate Scene whose qualities qualify every enacted clause via the scene-act ratio); (b) constitutional 'principles' are generalized wishes whose practical implementation forces conflict between wishes; (c) the strategic choice of circumference for any God-term ('freedom') determines what counts as its faithful extension; (d) ideal terms ('anarchism', 'freedom') belong to a heavenly realm where contradictions reconcile; their organizational counterparts ('syndicalism', 'capitalism') belong to a practical realm where contradictions force compromise; (e) political rhetoric is secular prayer — its function is to soften the sharply pointed and sharpen the pointless, not to describe. The chapter is the volume's methodological template: a demonstration that the pentad + ratios + substance vocabulary + four tropes can be deployed at document-corpus scale on a body of texts, producing diagnostic readings of the strategic choices each constitution-maker has made. This is the form the dissertation's game-studies operationalization chapter will inherit.

concepts.gloss: An anecdote 'sufficiently demarcated' for analysis and 'sufficiently complex' to defy simplist description; here Burke selects the Constitution itself because it is summational, converging, contemplable-as-statuesque, and substantively addressed to the question of what human relations are.

Burke's metaphor (taken from Coleridge's Biographia ch. XXII) for the relation between any narrower-and-wider pair of terms (matter/consciousness, understanding/reason, technology/science, routine/method). The narrower can be in apposition or opposition to the wider; idealists tend to read the narrower as misrepresentation of the wider.

A metonymic anecdote (e.g., railway terminal, electric-walking-graph) reduces the complex to the physical-and-simple; a synecdochic anecdote is part-for-whole (the expression about the eyes and mouth standing for the man). Only the synecdochic is representative; metonymic reductions become 'epicycles' once carried beyond their orbit.

Burke's metonymic test case: a Grand Central terminal makes mobility require fixity (schedules, calendars, bookkeeping). It dramatizes the wider/narrower-circle problem but is rejected as too physicalist; its clarity-of-metonymy is bought at the cost of dialectical scope.

concepts.term: Total war as candidate representative case
concepts.gloss: In modern conditions, war comes closest to the convergence-role once played by tribal totemic rites and Christian communion (the agape). Burke treats war as a constitutive-anecdote candidate while ultimately preferring 'the Constitution', because choosing war as constitutive would proclaim war as the essence of human relations.

A constitutive anecdote states what humanity substantially is; an admonitory anecdote stresses what humanity is in danger of becoming. Burke warns admonitory idioms (e.g., 'progress' doctrines that paint a warlike past) end up substantiating only what they meant to warn against, because they create no image but the enemy.

A directive (hortatory) ideal of peace is an annex to a statement of substance ('Men are essentially X; but let's have peace'); a constitutive Peace (Christ's Pacifist Manifesto, 'the Kingdom of Heaven is within you') makes peace identical with Being. Most pacifism is the former and is futuristic; only the latter is ontological.

Both religious and secular futurism merge present and future. Religious futurism reduces the future to the present ('find what now is within you and you have found what will be'); secular futurism reduces the present to the future ('find what will bring promises, and you have found what is worth doing now'). Investment, Puritan utility, and 'progress' are paradigmatic of the secular variant.

Burke's chapter-internal axis. A constitutive statement says 'it is so'; a futuristic statement says 'it should be' or 'it will be'. The chapter argues judgments rest on assumptions about scene (ontology), and only those grounded in ontology can be representative; futuristic idioms substitute future for present and reify the not-yet.

Reading Richard Wright's Native Son, Burke notes two kinds of epitomizing: the imagistic (Bigger's killing the rat as plot-foreshadow) and the conceptual (Marxist commentary). The pre-introduction is the conceptual summary that fits, after the fact, to the imagistic beginning.

The pentad needs nothing prior to it: it can be stated as a 'Let there be — and there was' beginning. Burke equates 'dramatic' and 'dialectical' and offers the pentad as the proper starting point for a study of motivation, immune to infinite regress of pre-introductions.

From con + statuere (to place, set), kin to stare (to stand). 'Constitution' inherits the entire substance-family lineage of GM-02 (substantia, hypostasis, instance, status) and therefore branches across all five pentad terms (act, scene, agent, agency, purpose).

Burke quotes Webster's Revised Unabridged: (1) the act of constituting/enactment; (2) state of being / form of being / texture / structure; (3) aggregate of inherited physical qualities; (4) aggregate of mental qualities / temperament; (5) fundamental organic law of a polity; (6) authoritative ordinance (esp. Roman-imperial or ecclesiastical). 'Constitution' covers all five pentad terms simultaneously.

Two functions of law: conservative codification of custom ('That sort of thing just isn't done') vs. innovative transformation of custom. In actual cases the two often invert: revolutionary changes in U.S. life were largely accomplished by men hiring legal talent to get innovations sanctioned in the name of tradition.

Herbert Read's anarchism, presented as 'vision', enjoys ideal immunity from practicability tests. Ideal anarchy is 'a state of absolute continuity approached through absolute discontinuity' where the lion and lamb lie down together; contradictions are reconcilable by definition because each ideal is a sovereign state.

The hyphenated term yokes an ideal first member to a 'worldly' second member: 'anarchism' is the Sermon-on-the-Mount stage of Read's church, 'syndicalism' is the Pauline-epistolary organizational stage. By Burke's reading, the pair adds to 'disorganized organization' — an oxymoron at the practical level.

Read equates poetry/anarchism/syndicalism vs. church/business/state/political-parties. The 'permanent revolution' minus Trotsky's political application. Read treats poetry-vs-business as in conflict but imagination-vs-reason as in equilibrium — the inconsistency Burke flags: 'rule of reason' smuggles authority back into an anti-authoritarian project.

Parkes's term: negative laissez-faire = hands-off; positive laissez-faire = 'hands-off à la hands-on'. He proposes universalizing property rights so every worker owns his job, achievable only by vigorous government interference. The 'reform vs. transform' ambiguity disguises a substantial change as preservation of principles.

Burke's diagrammatic spectrum (Parkes's vocabulary, made explicit): freedom > humanism > laissez-faire > free market > price system (money) > industrialism > capitalism. Each term restricts the circumference further; the ideal-pole and practical-pole are bridged by gradations that allow the rhetor to slip back and forth between heavenly and worldly registers.

By taking 'freedom' from the socially-given humanist tradition rather than from a theological or naturalistic source, Parkes can identify 'freedom' with 'free market' (no market exists in heaven or in the state of nature). The substance of a key term is determined by where its motivational ancestry is located.

A God-term designates 'the ultimate motivation, or substance, of a Constitutional frame'. For Parkes, money/the-price-system is the God-term: the qualities of the scene become 'second nature' to the agent, so a migration in response to wages is 'free will' even when socially compelled, by contrast with a dictator's transference of population. 'Where one can volunteer, there one is free.'

Two senses of 'reform': (i) a sinner reforms = abandons sin and returns to existing principles; (ii) reform = transform = change the principles themselves. Parkes calls government control of the labor and money markets 'reform of capitalism' while it actually transforms its substantive principles. The ambiguity is the rhetorical device that holds his Constitution together.

Constitutions are agonistic instruments: they imply an enemy. Coronation oaths, royal charters, the Bill of Rights all 'substantiate an ought' by reference to what should not be. A theorist's choice of opponent (Parkes's choice of Marxism as foil) shapes the substance of his own Constitution.

concepts.term: Constitutions — addressed by Agents to Agents
concepts.gloss: A Constitution is 'idealistic' in Burke's sense because its essential attributes belong to the term Agent: it is propounded by 'I/we' to 'you'. Two factors obscure this: (a) the addressee changes over historical time (originally a Crown, now a popularly elected government or a corporation); (b) commands grounded in 'natural law' merge what-must-be into what-is, so a futuristic gerundive ('inalienable') appears as a scenic ontological structure.

Burke's master concept: any explicit constitution is an enactment within a wider scene (social, natural, supernatural) whose qualities qualify the explicit enactment via the scene-act ratio. 'Positive' law tries to confine the circumference to the explicit document, but in practice the values, traditions and trends of business have served as the U.S. Constitution-behind-the-Constitution — making the Court 'representatives of business in a mood of mild self-criticism'.

concepts.term: Shifts in the locus of the 'representative'
concepts.gloss: In feudal thought the nobility is the 'representative' class (society's values culminate in it); after a 'fall' the representative part becomes the divisive part. Rights asserted against the Crown become rights asserted against the people's own government once the Crown is removed. The new opponent shapes the new substance.

Constitutional 'principles' work as eternal/universal only when raised to a sufficiently high level of generalization. The golden rule (= lex talionis converted from threat to cajolery) operates as a 'chapter-head' each tribe fills out differently. The U.S. Constitution's 'unchanging provisions adapted to the infinite variety of changing conditions' works the same way.

concepts.term: Limits and powers of a constitution
concepts.gloss: A constitution is in a sense supererogatory (rights it 'guarantees' you can already exercise need no guarantee; rights you cannot exercise no constitution can confer). Its real work is to single out certain motivational coordinates for attention. By centering attention on one calculus of motives, it labels Marxist, Fascist, naturalistic, theological, psychological motivations 'un-Constitutional'.

Coleridge's Utopian commune on the Susquehannah, designed to make virtue inevitable by 'aspheterism' (socializing of property, removing partisan interest as motive). Burke pairs Pantisocracy with the Ancient Mariner's blessing of the water-snakes 'unaware' — the dream of an act in which command and obedience are one, i.e., the merger of motive and impulse. Babbitt's objection that it lacks 'inner check' invites Coleridge's reply: Stoic virtue is virtue-in-spite-of-feelings, Christian virtue is moralization-of-feelings.

Coleridge's distinction: impulse = spontaneous action without external check; motive = arrested spontaneity. Burke uses the falling-man example — if pushed off a cliff and one clutches for something, the clutching is an act (motive); the descent is a natural event (no motive). The total act would be motive and impulse merged — an ideal incapable of realization in an imperfect world.

A public-act constitution is always representative of a vast complex body; even at the time of enactment many citizens participate only vicariously, and many not at all. The Declaration of Independence was unifying because it was a 'rejoinder to the Crown' (consubstantiality defined by shared opposition); the Constitution was less unifying because the unifying opponent had been abolished by the very act it culminated.

concepts.term: Principles of the conflict among principles
concepts.gloss: Two senses of 'principle': (i) principles-as-wishes = volitional, ideal, mutually independent in their pure ideality; (ii) principles-as-interrelationships = structural-mandatory facts about how wishes conflict when embodied in practical cases. The Constitution provides (i); the Court's judicial work is to handle (ii) by arbitration.

When constitutional wishes conflict in practical cases, what is mandatory is not obedience-to-the-text but a new act of arbitration: the Court must decide which wish gets preference, drawing motivation from the wider Constitution-behind-the-Constitution. Even an oration praising the Constitution must go outside the Constitution for reasons. Positive law's purity is self-undermining.

concepts.term: Some degree of constitutionality in every law
concepts.gloss: Because the U.S. Constitution contains an assortment of public and private rights and obligations, almost any proposed law gratifies some wish while frustrating another. A Court selecting only one principle to test a measure has not confronted the issue — it has chosen to favor one wish over its competitors. Hence the role of judicial 'higher law' arguments in the early Republic.

Burke's master distinction in constitutional hermeneutics: essentializing = select one clause and judge the measure against it (the litigant's strategy); proportional = test the measure against all wishes, naming a hierarchy among them. The proportional method is more judicious but harder; the essentializing method dominates because (a) nineteenth-century thought essentializes habitually, (b) judges are litigant-trained, (c) generalized principles produce 'where do you draw the line' problems that any partisan can extrapollate to absurdity.

concepts.term: Marshall's argument for the right of judicial review
concepts.gloss: Burke reads Marbury v. Madison (1803) as a paradigm of advocate-essentializing: Marshall selects as his test-case a clear conflict (an export-duty law vs. the explicit prohibition on export duties) and presents the decision as mandatory upon the Court. But the same Justice also established 'broad interpretation' (spirit-vs-letter) and the 'or' ambiguity in the Tenth Amendment ('to the States respectively, or to the people') opens proportional discretion that Marshall's own essentializing argument formally disallows.

concepts.term: The Constitution as a capitalist Constitution
concepts.gloss: Citing the Encyclopaedia of the Social Sciences and Beard's reading: U.S. constitutional guaranties protect against governmental abuse, not capitalist exploitation (the Thirteenth Amendment's bar on peonage is feudal-not-capitalist in target). Burke calls our Constitution 'essentially a capitalist Constitution, but one that points beyond capitalism' (amendment is unrestricted). Theological/metaphysical/naturalistic constitutions can claim total circumference; political constitutions cannot.

A constitution is itself a political act (not a scene), so it is partial. Every day since 1789 has been a day of 'emergency' in the sense that motivational ingredients not in the explicit document have been required. Party platforms are the most disparate constitutions of all: motivations-for-the-nonce, slung together to please each voting group; political-party structure developed outside the provisions of the Constitution.

concepts.term: Role of the President (FDR as case)
concepts.gloss: The President must find a unifying slogan/substance from which all his major policies can descend (the 'New Deal', 'All-Out Aid to the Democracies'). To remain a 'free agent' the President needs strong opposing groups to balance; if one weight on the seesaw goes flat, the candlestick at the centre becomes a 'prisoner to the heavier weight'. FDR's polio is treated speculatively as having taught him a 'distinction between action and motion' since he had to act by proxy.

Political language softens the sharply pointed and sharpens the pointless. A politician about to alienate an influential class will present the measure as reassuring and moderate ('a measure of partial control, done for their own good'); a politician forced to dampen public demand will thunder about scope while doing little. Roosevelt's 'death sentence' to holding companies told Burke the holding companies would in fact fare quite favorably.

concepts.term: War and the collectivistic nature of 'sacrifice'
concepts.gloss: A capitalist war economy resolves capitalism's wage-earner / wage-spender contradiction (the worker is both feared and flattered) by shrinking consumption and expanding destruction goods. But 'sacrifice' as motive cannot be individualist; war demands a collectivistic compensatory concept that capitalism has trained citizens to disbelieve. Fascism offers booty; the New Deal-era 'democracies' had only the promise of return to an unworkable order; Russia had collectivistic faith. The dialectic of motive-substance shifts under war-scene.

Burke reads Denis de Rougemont's Swiss-tradition argument that federalism is 'union in diversity' — not a 'system' (which is unitary in essence) but the harmonization of essentially different complementary parts. Burke supplements: economic interests at odds are antagonistic-not-complementary; the chapter closes by mapping federation's union-in-diversity onto Coleridge's fancy/imagination distinction. 'Unity of plurality' (e pluribus unum) is the dialectical formula. The Supreme Court oscillates between Jeffersonian states'-rights and Hamiltonian national-federation depending on which pole it elects to feature.

constitutional_vocabulary.operational_gloss: Ideal-pole term enjoying technical immunity to questions of practicability; defines a heavenly state where contradictions reconcile; Burke's diagnostic gloss = 'absolute continuity approached through absolute discontinuity'.

Oxymoron yoking ideal first member (anarchism) to organizational second member (syndicalism); Burke = 'disorganized organization'; reveals general structural problem: every embodiment of an ideal in a body of practice traduces it ('traduttore traditore').
Hands-off; classical 18th-century-liberal doctrine that state should only prevent injury between individuals; 'a government by laws rather than a government by men'.

Hands-off-with-a-measure-of-hands-on; Parkes's term for reforming-capitalism-without-abandoning-its-principles; relies on substantial/potential ambiguity to permit interventionist proposals under a non-interventionist label.

The God-term of the laissez-faire spectrum; counterpart of necessity; ancestrally locatable in heaven (theological), nature (naturalist), or socially-given tradition (Parkes's humanist choice). The strategic choice of ancestry determines what is permitted to be its faithful organizational extension.

Practical-pole of the laissez-faire spectrum; the most worldly term, against which the same theorist may frequently inveigh, retaining its 'virtues' by reference to the intermediate terms of the spectrum.

When monetary motivation has become 'second nature', the scene's compulsions appear internal to the agent; the migration-for-wages worker is 'free' relative to the dictator's transferred-population worker; 'Where one can volunteer, there one is free'. Money operates as a Constitutional ground-of-motivation for industrial capitalism.

'Union in diversity' — not a unitary system but harmonization of essentially-different complementary parts; the dialectical resolution of unity/plurality; mappable onto Coleridge's imagination/fancy axis. Treated as marriage (cherishing differences) not Gleichschaltung (forcing similarity).

Constitutive anecdote: states what the universe substantially is. Admonitory anecdote: stresses what humanity is in danger of becoming. Admonitory idioms create only enemy-image and risk substantiating what they warn against (progress-doctrine paradox).

The implicit scene-of-scenes (social, natural, supernatural) in which any explicit constitution is an enactment. By scene-act ratio its qualities qualify every clause. 'Positive' law tries to deny it; in the U.S. case the values and trends of business have functioned as it.

The modern act that comes closest to the synecdochic convergence-role once played by tribal totemic festivals and the Christian agape; if chosen as constitutive anecdote it makes war the essence of human relations, so Burke uses it only as a partial / heuristic anecdote.

Where the theorist locates a key term's motivational ancestry (heaven, nature, tradition) determines what is permitted to count as its faithful extension. Parkes's choice of humanist tradition for 'freedom' permits identification of freedom with free-market in a way theological or naturalist ancestries would not.

'Reform' has two senses: (i) return-to-existing-principles (sinner reforms); (ii) transform-the-principles. Theorists exploit the ambiguity to license substantial change while claiming continuity. The same ambiguity is central to constitutional 'broad interpretation' debate.

Constitutional 'principles' work eternally only when phrased at high enough generality (golden rule, 'welfare', 'general security'). Each particular case fills out the chapter-head differently. The level of generalization is the price of universality.
constitutional_vocabulary.scope: structural feature of any durable constitution

constitutional_vocabulary.operational_gloss: Essentializing = test a measure against one clause (advocate's method, Marshall in Marbury). Proportional = test against the recipe of all wishes, naming an explicit hierarchy among them (the judicious method). Burke's analytical preference is proportional, but practice favors essentializing.

Public political language functions like prayer: it softens the sharply pointed (drastic measures presented as moderate) and sharpens the pointless (modest measures thundered about with great noise). It is neither lying nor hypocrisy but a normal function of language under partisan conditions.

A directive idiom posits an ideal to aim at; a constitutive idiom posits a substance to share. Christ's Pacifist Manifesto is constitutive (Peace = Being); ordinary pacifism is directive (Peace is an annex tacked onto whatever else is said about substance).

An anecdote summational-and-converging that grounds the analytic terminology in something the analyst takes to be representative-of-human-relations. Must be synecdochic (part-for-whole), not metonymic (reduction-to-physical).

applied_dramatism_walkthrough.summary: GM-08 is the volume's master demonstration that the pentad is not a theoretical schema awaiting application but an analytical instrument deployable at document-corpus scale. Burke does not say 'a constitution features term X'; he shows, in worked cases, that any given constitution can be diagnosed by which pentad term its rhetorical strategy elects to feature in each move, and that the scene-act ratio is the master ratio of constitutional theory.

moves.move: Constitution as substance, substance as motive
moves.explanation: Burke's opening axiom: 'a thing's substance is that whereof it is constituted; hence a concern with substance is a concern with constitutionality'. The constitution-behind-the-Constitution is the scenic ultimate; every explicit constitutional act takes place within its circumference.

moves.move: Constitutions addressed by Agents to Agents
moves.explanation: A constitution is 'idealistic' (in Burke's sense from GM-05) because its definitional attributes belong to the term Agent: it is propounded by 'I/we' to 'you'. The visions of Read and Parkes are agent-projections cast as scene-statements.

A Constitution is itself an act — and a political (not theological/metaphysical) act is partial, embedded in a wider scene. The Declaration of Independence and the Constitution are paradigms of public acts whose unifying force is dialectically tied to the opponent each was addressed to.

The instruments of constitutional life — judicial review, the essentializing-vs-proportional choice, broad-vs-strict construction, party platforms, lobbies — are the means by which the agent's wishes become acts in the scene. Marshall's Marbury argument is an Agency-move masquerading as an Act-as-mandatory.

moves.move: Ends, ideals, the 'unwritten clause' of reconciliation
moves.explanation: The 'unwritten clause' of every ideal vision — that in this hypothetical realm all contradictions reconcile — is a Purpose-statement masquerading as a Scene-statement. The constitutive-vs-directive axis on Peace and the religious-vs-secular axis on futurism are explicit Purpose-debates.

moves.move: Scene-act ratio as master ratio of constitutional theory
moves.explanation: The chapter's most-used ratio: 'the quality of the situation in which we act qualifies our act' (book p.336). When the Constitution-behind-the-Constitution changes (industrial revolution, rise of monopolies, war emergency), the explicit Constitution's clauses must mean differently because the scene that gave them meaning has shifted. This is the dramatistic generator of the entire judicial-review debate.

moves.move: Agent-act ratio: idealistic Constitution presupposes idealistic agent
moves.explanation: Since constitutions are addressed by Agents to Agents, the constitution-maker's vision of the addressee shapes the wishes it can intelligibly propound; Read's anarcho-syndicalist Constitution presupposes an agent unmediated by father-figures, Parkes's positive-laissez-faire presupposes an agent already monetarily socialized.

Whether government interference is 'reform of capitalism' (preserves Purpose, changes Agency) or 'transform' (changes Purpose with Agency) is the central diagnostic question; Parkes exploits the agency-purpose ambiguity to relabel a transformation as a reform.

'Constitution' from con+statuere (stance family); 'inalienable rights' as gerundive masquerading as ontology; 'principle' as substantive-of-wish; 'second nature' as substantial-vs-potential merger. The entire Antinomies-of-Definition vocabulary is the analytic palette of GM-08.

Synecdoche (representative anecdote, part-for-whole) and metonymy (reduction, railway terminal) frame the methodological apparatus. Irony (positive-vs-negative laissez-faire) marks the constitutive contradictions of liberal substance. Metaphor (concentric circles, fencer statue, marriage-as-federation) is Burke's heuristic device.

A constitution-text 'features' a pentad term as the locus of motive; it does not omit the others. Read's anarcho-syndicalist text features Agent (autonomous-individual brotherhood); Parkes's text features Scene (the market as ground) by way of money-as-God-term; the U.S. Constitution features Agent (popular sovereignty) and Scene (business as Constitution-behind-the-Constitution) in tension.

applied_dramatism_walkthrough.template_for_dissertation: The dissertation's game-design operationalization chapter inherits exactly this method: a worked corpus of game-design theories analyzed (a) for which pentad term each features as locus of motive, (b) for which dyadic ratios it most relies upon, (c) for which God-term (= terminological ultimate substance) it implicitly invokes, (d) for its strategic choice of circumference (the implicit Constitution-behind-the-Theory), (e) for whether its claims are constitutive (claim-of-substance) or admonitory/directive (claim-of-aim), and (f) for the essentializing-vs-proportional structure of its hermeneutic. Ludology, narratology, embodied-cognition game studies and procedural-rhetoric become recognizable as distinct constitutional projects, each diagnosable as a partial constitution-text with its own God-term, opponent, and shape of unity-in-diversity.

positions.statement: A constitution is a substance and therefore a structure of motives; 'substance' and 'motivation' are convertible (Wechselbegriffe).
A representative anecdote must be synecdochic (part-for-whole) rather than metonymic (reduction-to-physical-or-simple); only the synecdochic anecdote can yield representative terms.

The scene-act ratio is the master ratio of constitutional theory: because the explicit Constitution is an enactment within a wider scene whose qualities change, the Constitution's clauses must be interpreted in light of the Constitution-behind-the-Constitution.
Constitutions are agonistic instruments: they substantiate their 'ought' against an opponent's 'ought-not'. Their shape and unifying force depend dialectically on the opponent's character.

Whenever an ideal Constitutional term is embodied in an organizational practice, the practice translates ideal-mergers into practical-contradictions; the embodiment is either a 'copy' or a 'betrayal' of the original.

Because most legislation gratifies some constitutional wishes while frustrating others, judicial review proper requires the proportional method (with an explicit hierarchy among wishes), not the essentializing method that selects one clause for combat.

Political rhetoric is a secular variant of prayer: it softens the sharply pointed and sharpens the pointless. To use language consistently for description rather than stylistic refurbishment in such cases is nearly impossible.
A war economy resolves the capitalist wage-earner / wage-spender contradiction at the price of demanding a collectivistic 'sacrifice' motive that capitalism has trained citizens to disbelieve.

Federation is the dialectical resolution of unity and plurality: not a unitary 'system' but the harmonization of essentially-different complementary parts, mappable onto Coleridge's imagination/fancy axis.

philosophers_cited.name: Coleridge
philosophers_cited.role: PRIMARY interlocutor; cited for Biographia's concentric-circles dialectic (ch. XXII), motive/impulse distinction, Pantisocracy project, Ancient Mariner's blessing-of-water-snakes, fancy/imagination distinction, comment on Burke (Edmund) on principles-and-expediency, Aids to Reflection on Stoic vs. Christian virtue.

philosophers_cited.name: Marx (Karl) + Engels
philosophers_cited.role: Foil for Parkes's laissez-faire defense; Marxist 'inevitability' as rival God-term; 'freedom is the knowledge of necessity'; the Communist Manifesto as 'pre-Constitution'; proletariat as primus inter pares.

philosophers_cited.name: Aristotle
philosophers_cited.role: Passing on 'final cause' as 'prime mover' (basis for Burke's resolution of beginnings/endings); on politics; on substance.

philosophers_cited.name: Heraclitus
philosophers_cited.role: 'Strife' and 'War' as synonyms for Universal Fire; everything flows; fire as universal currency 'as goods for gold and gold for goods' (passage Burke connects to money-as-Constitutional-substance).

philosophers_cited.name: Spinoza
philosophers_cited.role: Necessity from within = freedom; Marxist appropriation of this principle; necessity-as-second-nature.

philosophers_cited.name: Hegel
philosophers_cited.role: Implicit in Marxist dialectical inheritance; in Burke's framing of historical change as dialectical (give-and-take of combat).

philosophers_cited.name: Locke (Hobbes implied)
philosophers_cited.role: Background to constitutional theory; the social contract tradition; substance-discussion lineage.

philosophers_cited.name: Bentham
philosophers_cited.role: Used 'interest' as Coleridge used 'motive'; ethics-and-pragmatism predecessor.

philosophers_cited.name: Babbitt (Irving)
philosophers_cited.role: 'Inner check' doctrine of virtue; Coleridge anticipates the objection that the Ancient Mariner's blessing lacks an inner check.

philosophers_cited.name: Adam Smith
philosophers_cited.role: Capitalist dialectic: individual aggrandizement = public benefit; cited as the philosophy of peace-by-amassing that the war economy must invert into peace-by-sacrifice.

philosophers_cited.name: Rousseau
philosophers_cited.role: Volonté générale on the macrocosm-microcosm pattern; common substance defined against a common external enemy (the feudal sovereign).

philosophers_cited.name: Augustine
philosophers_cited.role: Political theology; the merger of secular and religious law under Constantine, in which Augustine plays a stylistic role.

philosophers_cited.name: Leibniz
philosophers_cited.role: Anticipator of Coleridge's union-in-diversity dialectic; cited as the deeper source of de Rougemont's federalist concept.

philosophers_cited.name: Herbert Read
philosophers_cited.role: Author of Poetry and Anarchism; case study #1; the anarcho-syndicalist visionary whose hyphenated term Burke diagnoses as oxymoron.

philosophers_cited.name: H. B. Parkes

tensions.statement: Every constitution that claims to deliver an ideal must embody that ideal in an organizational practice; the embodiment is necessarily a translation that either betrays or copies the ideal. The chapter cannot resolve this tension because it is structural (book pp.345-349).

Burke's analytical preference is proportional interpretation, but the actual practice of judicial review (and political-platform construction) is overwhelmingly essentializing. Marshall established both the right of review (essentializing) and the broad-construction principle (which calls for proportional); these are in latent tension within the same juridical tradition (book pp.380-388).

If war is selected as constitutive anecdote, war becomes the essence of human relations; if peace is selected as constitutive, peace must be ontological (Christ-style) not directive (pacifist-style), but then it requires an exceptional 'essentially peaceful' author. The chapter's resolution — choose 'Constitution' as anecdote and give 'the purification of war' rather than 'the anecdote of peace' — sits uneasily between the two poles (book pp.328-338).

Positive law tries to make the explicit Constitution the sole criterion of motivational judgment, but every act has motives lying partially beyond the document. Hence 'Constitution makes extra-constitutionality mandatory' — the Court must constantly draw on the wider circumference, undermining the very theory of positive law on which its own role is founded (book pp.376-378).

Capitalism's individualist motive cannot underwrite the sacrifice required by a war economy; war demands a collectivist compensatory concept (Fascism = booty; Russia = communist faith). The U.S. New Deal's mild collectivism was deliberately not refurbished for World War II out of fear that it would foreclose 'business as usual' afterward (book pp.394-398).

Federation is union-in-diversity, but the accentual difference between 'unity in diversity' and 'unity in diversity' tracks the difference between imagination and fancy (Coleridge), Hamiltonian and Jeffersonian readings of 'United States', and the Supreme Court's discretion to sanction or nullify the same law from either pole (book pp.398-401).
